title: Public leaderboards can't measure what a model can actually do — third-party evaluation is the real need
dek: Llama 4 looked astonishing on public leaderboards but underperformed on Vals's private held-out set — the gap between self-reported scores and real capability is spawning an independent evaluation industry.
why: Medium information density; the first half covers evaluation methodology, while the second half on enterprise token spending and the division of policy labor is more valuable.
who: Engineering leads choosing AI models and coding agents for their companies, CTOs who need to justify AI ROI to their boards, and practitioners watching AI policy and evaluation standards.
skip: The intro and introductions from 0:00-2:03 can be skipped.

points.h: Llama 4 exposed the crack in self-reported scores
points.body: Rayan gives the concrete case: when Meta released Llama 4, the model was in fact underperforming on Vals's private held-out benchmark, yet on all the major public benchmarks — because the questions and the grading criteria are open source — it showed astonishing capability. That gap shows a huge disconnect between what labs self-report and what third-party, high-quality, high-signal benchmarks measure. Rayan thinks the labs themselves understand this, and that what they want is a rational buyer's market: when you're spending billions of dollars training a new model, you need substantive evidence pointing to progress, not to be the sole judge of your own work.

points.h: An evaluator can't also sell training data
points.body: One key early decision at Vals was to never sell training data to labs. Rayan says this is the direction they're constantly pushed in — when partnering with a new lab, the other side will propose buying training data, which is a lucrative business, and many companies in the industry already make gimmicky benchmarks to sell data; that has become their go-to-market. He draws an analogy to the audit industry: if the same people doing the audit are also consulting for the company, the incentive structure is muddled, and it ends up as paying to pass the audit — in AI, paying to win the leaderboard. Ben adds that this is a bit like MPAA ratings — what is art, what is pornography, where the line is, the definition itself shifts over time, and ultimately it depends on enough people in the industry converging on a consensus, rather than a narrow, easily-gamed rule like "solve this problem and you're at this level."

points.h: Evaluation is moving from millions of samples to a few tasks
points.body: Rayan describes a structural shift: the more complex the evaluation, the smaller the sample size, but the more criteria there are for judging the output. Early on, something like ImageNet was a few million images doing basic classification, with a one-to-one mapping between input and output; now it might be a far smaller number of tasks like "generate 50 full-stack web apps," but the machinery for evaluating the output is far more complex. The infrastructure layer changes accordingly — you now have to test a model's ability to run for hours, days, or even weeks, and the infrastructure has to be stable enough that if a request fails you can retry from that point rather than rerunning the whole trajectory. He thinks this trend will continue as more complex work gets folded into evaluation.

points.h: Token spending may exceed salary spending
points.body: Rayan tells the case of a Fortune 10 company: they gave engineers a Claude Code budget of about $100 a day, and because the quota reset at 4pm, the most productive working hours became 4 to 6pm, with a dead zone in the afternoon when people went for walks and coffee. The company recently raised the quota to $300 per person — almost as if an employee's salary had turned into tokens. Rayan's judgment: mispricing of intelligence is happening at every layer, engineers don't know how to allocate that $100 for maximum productivity, companies set quotas arbitrarily, and Anthropic is supporting all of it on thin margins. When token spending starts to exceed salary spending, enterprises will have to argue ROI more seriously than they have in the past six months.

points.h: The most expensive model isn't necessarily the biggest bill
points.body: Rayan points out that today it's still hard to say the best OpenAI model or the best Anthropic model is necessarily the best fit for your codebase, and many counterintuitive cases only become clear by running evaluations. The middle layer of options has become very complicated: Anthropic has Opus and Sonnet, plus Luna and Terra; Luna is very competitive on cost, MewSpark is also cheap, 1.2 is very strong, and there are growing open-source models you can self-host. He gives a concrete counterexample: in many cases Sonnet is more expensive than Opus, because it's so token-hungry, and if you operate on a "use it if it feels applicable" basis, you may end up spending more.

points.h: The experiment that burned $150,000 of tokens in a month
points.body: The product ValSmith came out of a pit Vals dug for itself. Rayan ran a token maxing experiment, getting the team unlimited access to certain coding tools for a month, and in hindsight they were consuming 1 to 2 billion tokens a day, with a peak day where one engineer burned 6 billion. He did the math: that month they spent roughly $1.5 million worth of tokens — it was free, but in reality it was 10 times employee salaries, not a 50-50 split. So they dug through traces and GitHub repos, built ValSmith, and found some counterintuitive conclusions: Cognition's Devon tool is actually very token-efficient, so it got adopted more; in some scenarios subscription pricing is a better deal than per-token pricing. This approach later became their operating strategy.

points.h: Government sets the rules, third parties judge whether they were broken
points.body: Ben lays out the division of policy labor clearly: government receives a lot of warnings from the big labs — this thing will be used for biohacking, it will be a cybersecurity risk — so what government needs to do is first clarify what it's afraid of, then ask two questions: does the model have this capability, and can someone steer the model into doing this. Ben thinks government is particularly unsuited to doing the latter evaluation, especially over time; it's not a good government function. But government is very good at making rules, because it can enforce them. So the ideal combination is government making and enforcing the rules, with capable private companies telling it whether the rules have been broken. He also mentions a phenomenon: big labs are starting to say the model has this capability and can be steered to do bad things, so we won't let anyone use it — only we will, and we'll make sure our own people don't steer it to do bad things — and even then it doesn't always work.

points.h: Nuclear arms control's "trust but verify" is the template for AI
points.body: Rayan says that from an idealistic standpoint, he's surprised by the enormous investment in sovereign AI — from a god's-eye view, building this many data centers, duplicating data engineering pipelines, and training these enormous models is extremely inefficient, and it could have been consolidated. But the reality is that countries are ramping up sovereign AI buildout, which requires a shared language for communicating evaluation frameworks and risk alignment. He quotes Reagan's "trust but verify," noting that Xi Jinping and Trump will meet next month, signs of trust are appearing, but there's no clear method for the verification half. In nuclear arms control, verification relies on overflights, letting one country audit another's nuclear stockpile; if AI carries societal or existential risk, a shared language of evaluation is likewise needed to accomplish verification.
